error_modes.label: CONTINUOUS VISUAL LOOKOUT THROUGHOUT THE SORTIE

texts.0: SP, due to complacency in a familiar profile that replaced an active scan, did not check the surrounding space uninterruptedly during flight. The lookout lapsed for extended periods with attention held inside the cockpit, and traffic called by the controlling agency was never acquired visually. IP took the controls and maneuvered the aircraft to open separation from an aircraft SP had not seen.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that settled into a fixed forward sector, checked the surrounding space only at long intervals. Entire quadrants, in particular high and behind the wing line, were left uncleared for the greater part of each maneuver, which is at the limit of what the standard allows. SP reestablished an effective scan only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the maneuver being flown, allowed the visual scan to become irregular at times. Two or three sectors were left uncleared during the working phase, short of the tolerance limit but below the required continuity. SP recognized the omission and reestablished a full scan pattern in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP checked the surrounding space continuously throughout the sortie. The scan covered all sectors in a systematic sequence, including above, below and behind the wing line, and was maintained both between and during maneuvers. No sector was left uncleared before a maneuver was commenced.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted and disciplined lookout for the whole flight, with the scan sequence unaffected by workload or by the demands of the maneuvers being flown. Sectors were cleared before they were needed rather than after the fact. Every aircraft in the vicinity was acquired visually before it became a factor.
texts.marginal: SP checked the surrounding space to the required standard, but the scan tended to narrow toward the forward sector whenever task loading increased. The rear and high sectors were cleared at noticeably longer intervals than the rest. SP is expected to keep the scan sequence uniform across all sectors so that lookout does not thin out under workload.

texts_at.0: SP worked the continuous visual lookout, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP checked the surrounding space inside the code 1 band, one sector going uncleared for longer than the standard allows before the scan sequence was reestablished. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the scan sequence uniform under workload so no sector is left for the same length of time again.
texts_at.2: SP checked the surrounding space inside the code 2 band, correcting a scan that had grown irregular during the working phase before it was fully reestablished. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice the irregularity a little sooner so fewer sectors are affected before the correction.
texts_at.3: SP checked the surrounding space continuously, with the scan covering all sectors in sequence and only a brief irregularity appearing during one maneuver before it was corrected. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold the sequence steady through that phase as well.

texts_above.1: SP checked the surrounding space continuously through the sortie, with one sector going uncleared for longer than the standard allows. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a scan that had started to narrow under workload and widened it again without prompting, covering every sector before the next maneuver was commenced. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good lookout discipline across the sortie.
texts_above.3: SP checked the surrounding space continuously throughout the sortie, with the scan sequence covering every sector, including above, below and behind the wing line, and holding steady even as task loading increased. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good lookout discipline across the sortie.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted and disciplined lookout for the whole flight, with the scan sequence unaffected by workload and every aircraft in the vicinity acquired before it became a factor. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent lookout discipline across the sortie.

error_modes.label: CLEARING IN THE AIRPORT TRAFFIC PATTERN

texts.0: SP, due to attention concentrated on the runway aim point, did not check the surrounding space while in the airport traffic pattern. Base and final legs were flown without any check of the sectors from which converging traffic could arrive, and preceding traffic in the pattern went unseen. IP intervened on the controls to break out of the pattern and reestablish spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout limited to the single aircraft being followed, cleared the pattern only in the direction of flight. The sectors toward the crosswind and the pattern entry were not checked before turning, leaving the position of other pattern traffic unknown to SP, at the limit of the acceptable standard. Clearing improved only after the IP called the traffic verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a check made after rather than before the turn was initiated, cleared the pattern late on one occasion. The delay left the sector being turned into unchecked for a short period, between the two tolerance levels rather than at the limit. SP identified the omission, cleared the sector and adjusted the turn without any intervention.
texts.3: SP cleared the surrounding space before every turn in the airport traffic pattern. Traffic ahead and behind was kept visually acquired and the sectors toward the pattern entry were checked before each leg change. Pattern spacing was adjusted on the basis of the visual picture rather than on assumption.
texts.4: SP kept the whole traffic pattern visually mapped at all times, with each turn preceded by a deliberate clearing check of the sector to be entered. The position of every other aircraft in the pattern was known and used to plan the spacing. Clearing remained complete even while flying the configuration changes.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the airport traffic pattern within the standard, but the checks were concentrated on the aircraft immediately ahead and gave thinner coverage of traffic joining the pattern. The clearing check preceding base was brief. SP is expected to extend the pattern check to the entry sectors so that joining traffic is detected as early as traffic being followed.

texts_at.0: SP practiced clearing in the traffic pattern, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP cleared the pattern before each turn inside the code 1 band, one sector toward the pattern entry going unchecked before the traffic picture was confirmed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to extend the pattern check to the entry sectors so joining traffic is detected as early as traffic being followed.
texts_at.2: SP cleared the pattern before each turn inside the code 2 band, correcting a check made after rather than before one turn was initiated. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to complete the check before commencing the turn on every occasion.
texts_at.3: SP cleared the surrounding space before every turn in the airport traffic pattern, with the sectors toward the pattern entry checked before each leg change and only a momentary delay on one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to remove that last delay so every check leads its turn.

texts_above.1: SP cleared the pattern before each turn, with one sector toward the pattern entry going unchecked. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified a check that had slipped to after a turn had begun and cleared the sector immediately, adjusting the turn without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound pattern clearing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP cleared the surrounding space before every turn in the airport traffic pattern, keeping traffic ahead and behind visually acquired and checking the sectors toward the pattern entry before each leg change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pattern clearing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept the whole traffic pattern visually mapped at all times, with each turn preceded by a deliberate clearing check and the position of every other aircraft known and used to plan spacing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional pattern clearing discipline.

error_modes.label: TIMELY DETECTION OF NEARBY TRAFFIC AND SEPARATION

texts.0: SP, due to a lookout that was directed only along the flight path, did not detect nearby moving aircraft in time and did not maintain appropriate separation. Converging traffic closed to a distance where the situation had become hazardous before it was seen, and SP had no assessment of its relative motion. IP intervened on the controls to reestablish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan interval too long for the traffic density in the area, detected nearby aircraft only when they were already close abeam. Separation was reduced to the minimum still acceptable and no margin remained for a further change of the other aircraft's flight path. SP repositioned only after the IP pointed out the traffic verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to attention retained on the maneuver being set up, detected nearby traffic later than the visual picture allowed. Separation was reduced but stayed clearly short of a hazardous condition, between the two tolerance levels. SP assessed the relative motion and adjusted the flight path in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP detected nearby moving aircraft in good time and maintained appropriate separation from each of them. Relative motion was assessed correctly on first acquisition and the flight path was adjusted early enough that no hazardous situation could develop. Traffic once acquired was kept in the scan until it was no longer a factor.
texts.4: SP acquired every nearby aircraft well before it became a factor and maintained separation with a comfortable margin at all times. Relative motion was assessed immediately and used to plan the maneuvering, so that no adjustment was ever made under time pressure. Traffic detection consistently preceded the radio call reporting it.
texts.marginal: SP detected nearby traffic and maintained separation within the standard, but acquisition came later than the conditions allowed and the resulting margins were smaller than necessary. The pattern indicates that relative motion is assessed only after the aircraft has been in view for some time. SP is expected to acquire traffic earlier so that separation is planned rather than preserved by a late adjustment.

texts_at.0: SP practiced detecting nearby traffic and separation, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP detected nearby traffic and maintained separation inside the code 1 band, acquiring one aircraft only when it was already close abeam before the margin was assessed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to acquire traffic earlier so separation is planned rather than preserved by a late adjustment.
texts_at.2: SP detected nearby traffic and maintained separation inside the code 2 band, correcting a detection that came later than the visual picture allowed on one occasion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to assess relative motion as soon as a contact is acquired rather than after a further interval.
texts_at.3: SP detected nearby moving aircraft in good time and maintained appropriate separation, assessing relative motion correctly on first acquisition with only one contact picked up a little later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to close that one gap so every contact is acquired equally early.

texts_above.1: SP detected nearby traffic and maintained separation, acquiring one aircraft only when it was already close abeam. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP assessed the relative motion of a contact acquired later than planned and adjusted the flight path in good time, without any intervention needed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid traffic detection and separation judgment.
texts_above.3: SP detected nearby moving aircraft in good time and maintained appropriate separation from each of them, assessing relative motion correctly on first acquisition and adjusting the flight path early enough that no hazardous situation could develop. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise traffic detection and separation judgment.
texts_above.4: SP acquired every nearby aircraft well before it became a factor and maintained separation with a comfortable margin at all times, with detection consistently preceding the radio call reporting it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior traffic detection and separation judgment.

error_modes.label: AVOIDANCE ACTION AND AIRCRAFT CONTROL DURING THE MANEUVER

texts.0: SP, due to a delayed assessment of the developing conflict, did not take the action required to avoid entering a hazardous situation. No avoidance maneuver was initiated against traffic already converging, and when SP finally reacted the input was abrupt and the aircraft was not kept under control within the parameters of the maneuver. IP took the controls to complete the avoidance and recover the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over whether the traffic was a factor, initiated the avoidance maneuver only when the conflict was fully developed. The maneuver produced the required separation, but only just, and aircraft control during it was coarse, at the limit of what remains acceptable. SP acted only after the IP directed the avoidance verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a late decision on the direction of the avoidance turn, maneuvered later than the geometry allowed. The turn was made with more bank than the situation required, though the aircraft remained under positive control and separation was never in question. SP corrected the technique on the subsequent avoidance without any intervention.
texts.3: SP took timely action and maneuvered as required to avoid a midair collision. The avoidance turn was initiated early, in the direction that increased separation fastest, and was flown with the aircraft under full control throughout. SP returned to the planned profile once the conflict had passed.
texts.4: SP anticipated the developing conflict and resolved it with a small, early flight path change that made an avoidance maneuver unnecessary. Aircraft control remained precise throughout, with no excursion in attitude, altitude or airspeed. The resolution was communicated and the profile resumed without disruption.
texts.marginal: SP took avoidance action within the standard, but the decision to maneuver came close to the point where a larger input would have been needed. Control of the aircraft during the avoidance was adequate though not smooth. SP is expected to decide and act earlier, so that avoidance can be achieved with a gentle flight path change rather than an aggressive one.

texts_at.0: SP practiced avoidance action and aircraft control, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP took action to avoid a midair collision inside the code 1 band, the avoidance maneuver producing the required separation only just before aircraft control was fully regained. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to decide and act earlier so avoidance can be achieved with a gentle flight path change rather than an aggressive one.
texts_at.2: SP took action to avoid a midair collision inside the code 2 band, correcting a turn flown with more bank than the geometry required on one occasion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to size the avoidance turn to the geometry from the first input.
texts_at.3: SP took timely action and maneuvered as required, initiating the avoidance turn early in the direction that increased separation fastest with the aircraft under full control throughout. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to shave a little more time off the decision so the margin grows further.

texts_above.1: SP took action to avoid a midair collision, the avoidance maneuver producing the required separation only just in time. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected the technique on a subsequent avoidance after an earlier turn used more bank than the situation required, with separation never in question. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady avoidance-maneuver technique.
texts_above.3: SP took timely action and maneuvered as required to avoid a midair collision, initiating the turn early in the direction that increased separation fastest and flying it with the aircraft under full control throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined avoidance-maneuver technique.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the developing conflict and resolved it with a small, early flight path change that made a full avoidance maneuver unnecessary, with aircraft control remaining precise throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate avoidance-maneuver technique.

error_modes.label: R/T MONITORING AND BUILD-UP OF SITUATIONAL AWARENESS

texts.0: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the other traffic, did not monitor the R/T effectively or continuously. Position reports from other aircraft operating in the same area were not processed, so no mental picture of the surrounding traffic was built and an imminent airborne threat went unrecognized. IP had to take control and deconflict the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to attention absorbed by the maneuver in progress, monitored the R/T only intermittently. Several calls affecting the area in use were missed and SP could not state the position of traffic that had reported nearby, which is at the limit of the acceptable standard. The traffic picture was rebuilt only after the IP repeated the information verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a transmission being prepared while another station was reporting, missed part of the R/T picture. One position report from traffic in the adjacent block was not assimilated, a shortfall short of the tolerance limit. SP requested clarification and restored an accurate traffic picture in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP monitored the R/T effectively and continuously throughout the sortie. Calls from other aircraft were used to build situational awareness of who was operating where, and the traffic picture was updated as each report was received. Visual search was directed toward the sectors indicated by the radio picture before any threat could develop.
texts.4: SP maintained a complete and current radio picture of all traffic in the operating area for the whole flight, integrating each report into the visual search plan. Potential conflicts were identified from the R/T well before they became visible and were resolved by planning rather than by reaction. SP could state at any time the position and intention of the other aircraft on frequency.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the R/T to the required standard, but the traffic picture built from it was retained only for the aircraft in the immediate vicinity and faded for the rest. Calls concerning adjacent areas were heard without being used. SP is expected to convert the whole radio picture into an active search plan so that situational awareness extends beyond the nearest aircraft.

texts_at.0: SP worked R/T monitoring and situational awareness, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP monitored the R/T and built situational awareness inside the code 1 band, the position of one reported aircraft not recalled until the picture was repeated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to convert the whole radio picture into an active search plan rather than retaining only the nearest contact.
texts_at.2: SP monitored the R/T and built situational awareness inside the code 2 band, correcting a gap left by one position report not fully assimilated. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to request clarification the moment a report is missed rather than after the picture is needed.
texts_at.3: SP monitored the R/T effectively and continuously, updating the traffic picture as each report was received with only one call needing a second listen before it was placed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to place that call correctly on the first hearing as well.

texts_above.1: SP monitored the R/T and built situational awareness, with the position of one reported aircraft not recalled from the first call. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP requested clarification after one position report was not fully assimilated and restored an accurate traffic picture without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good R/T-based situational awareness.
texts_above.3: SP monitored the R/T effectively and continuously throughout the sortie, using calls from other aircraft to build situational awareness and directing the visual search toward the sectors the radio picture indicated. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good R/T-based situational awareness.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a complete and current radio picture of all traffic in the operating area, integrating each report into the visual search plan and identifying potential conflicts from the R/T well before they became visible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent R/T-based situational awareness.

texts.0: SP, due to a flight path flown without reference to the developing cloud, did not maintain the appropriate VFR distance from clouds. The aircraft was flown close enough to the cloud edge that visual reference and the ability to see and avoid traffic emerging from it were lost. IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft clear of the cloud.
texts.1: SP, due to a late recognition of the cloud build-up along the intended track, maintained only the minimum VFR distance from clouds. The margin was at the limit throughout the working phase and left no allowance for the cloud growing further. SP repositioned only after being directed verbally by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a maneuver commenced without checking the exit heading against the cloud, closed on the cloud edge more than planned. The VFR distance was reduced but remained clearly greater than the minimum. SP recognized the trend, moved the working area and restored a comfortable margin without any intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained appropriate VFR distance from clouds throughout the flight. The working area and maneuver entries were positioned so that every recovery heading kept the aircraft well clear of cloud. Visual reference to the horizon and to the ground was preserved at all times.
texts.4: SP planned each maneuver around the cloud picture, so that the VFR distance from clouds remained generous in every axis and required no repositioning. The cloud development was tracked continuously and anticipated in the choice of entry headings. Visual reference was never in question at any point of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP maintained VFR distance from clouds within the standard, but the working area was set up closer to the cloud edge than the available airspace required. Margins were adequate on entry and reduced on exit from the maneuvers. SP is expected to position the maneuvering area so that the cloud clearance is preserved on the recovery heading as well as on the entry.

texts_at.0: SP worked VFR distance from clouds, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the appropriate VFR distance from clouds inside the code 1 band, the margin sitting at the limit through the working phase before the area was reassessed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to position the working area with a wider margin so it does not depend on the cloud staying still.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the appropriate VFR distance from clouds inside the code 2 band, correcting a margin reduced by a maneuver commenced without checking the exit heading against the cloud. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to check the exit heading against the cloud before every entry, not only after closing on it.
texts_at.3: SP maintained appropriate VFR distance from clouds throughout the flight, with the working area positioned to keep the recovery heading well clear on all but one maneuver. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to apply the same margin to that maneuver as well.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the appropriate VFR distance from clouds, with the margin sitting at the limit through the working phase. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the aircraft closing on the cloud edge more than planned and moved the working area, restoring a comfortable margin without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound cloud clearance planning.
texts_above.3: SP maintained appropriate VFR distance from clouds throughout the flight, positioning the working area and maneuver entries so every recovery heading kept the aircraft well clear of cloud. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed cloud clearance planning.
texts_above.4: SP planned each maneuver around the cloud picture so the VFR distance remained generous in every axis, tracking the cloud development continuously and anticipating it in the choice of entry headings. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional cloud clearance planning.

error_modes.label: ATTENTION ALLOCATION BETWEEN CLEARING AND AIRCRAFT CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to workload distribution that left clearing, flying and transmitting to be done at the same time, did not allocate attention correctly during the clearing task. Either the lookout stopped while the aircraft was flown, or the aircraft state went unmonitored while SP looked out, and the aircraft was not maintained under control during the visual check. IP intervened on the controls to recover the flight parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to shed a secondary cockpit task when the traffic situation demanded a lookout, divided attention poorly between clearing and aircraft control. Each outside check produced a noticeable excursion in attitude or altitude, and clearing was suspended entirely whenever the aircraft had to be corrected, which is at the limit of the standard. Balance was restored only after the IP prompted SP verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a lookout sequence not matched to the phase of the maneuver, allowed attention to concentrate outside for longer than the aircraft state permitted. Small deviations in altitude and heading developed during the visual checks, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized the imbalance, shortened the outside intervals and restored the crosscheck in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP allocated attention correctly between the visual check, the R/T and the control of the aircraft. Clearing was performed in short, complete sweeps interleaved with the instrument crosscheck, and the aircraft was maintained under control throughout. Neither task was allowed to displace the other.
texts.4: SP integrated clearing, R/T monitoring and aircraft control into a single continuous routine, with no detectable cost to any of the three. Outside sweeps were complete and the flight parameters remained stable to the accuracy flown between them. Attention allocation stayed effective even during the highest workload phases of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP allocated attention between clearing and aircraft control within the standard, but the outside sweeps were long enough that small parameter deviations began to appear before the crosscheck was resumed. The tendency is toward one task at a time rather than an interleaved routine. SP is expected to shorten and repeat the outside checks so that lookout and aircraft control are sustained together.

texts_at.0: SP worked attention allocation between clearing and control, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP allocated attention between clearing and aircraft control inside the code 1 band, one outside check producing a noticeable excursion before the crosscheck was resumed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to shorten and repeat the outside checks so lookout and aircraft control are sustained together.
texts_at.2: SP allocated attention between clearing and aircraft control inside the code 2 band, correcting a small deviation that appeared during one visual check before the crosscheck was resumed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to match the lookout sequence to the phase of the maneuver a little more closely.
texts_at.3: SP allocated attention correctly between the visual check, the R/T and the control of the aircraft, performing clearing in short, complete sweeps with only one interval running slightly longer than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep that interval as short as the others.

texts_above.1: SP allocated attention between clearing and aircraft control, with one outside check producing a noticeable excursion. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an imbalance between the outside sweeps and the instrument crosscheck and shortened the outside intervals without prompting, restoring the crosscheck in good time. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent attention allocation between clearing and control.
texts_above.3: SP allocated attention correctly between the visual check, the R/T and the control of the aircraft, performing clearing in short, complete sweeps interleaved with the instrument crosscheck so neither task displaced the other. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined attention allocation between clearing and control.
texts_above.4: SP integrated clearing, R/T monitoring and aircraft control into a single continuous routine, with flight parameters remaining stable to the accuracy flown between the outside sweeps even during the highest workload phases. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless attention allocation between clearing and control.

error_modes.label: SECTORED VISUAL SCAN WITH FOCUS ON A DISTANT POINT

texts.0: SP, due to a lookout swept continuously across the canopy instead of a search of one arc of approximately 20-30 degrees at a time, did not clear the surrounding space in a manner capable of producing a detection. No arc was held long enough for the eye to focus on a distant point within it, so an aircraft inside the searched area was looked at without ever being acquired. IP took the controls and maneuvered the aircraft clear of traffic that SP had scanned across twice.
texts.1: SP, due to a search divided into arcs far wider than the 20-30 degrees the technique calls for, did not focus on a distant point within each arc for the 3-5 seconds required. Each sweep of the canopy was completed in a couple of seconds, so the whole surrounding space was covered by eye movement alone with no dwell in any sector, which is at the limit of what the standard allows. SP began to search arc by arc only after being prompted verbally by the IP on several occasions.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan rate that accelerated whenever the maneuver demanded attention, held some arcs well short of the 3-5 second focus on a distant point. Two or three sectors in each sweep received a passing glance rather than a search, short of the tolerance limit but below the technique required. SP recognized that the scan had become a sweep, slowed it back to discrete arcs and restored the dwell in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP searched the surrounding space one arc of approximately 20-30 degrees at a time, focusing on a distant point within each arc for 3-5 seconds before moving to the next. The sequence of arcs covered the full field available from the cockpit and was repeated at a steady rate throughout the sortie. Traffic in the searched sectors was acquired at a range that left the situation entirely unhurried.
texts.4: SP applied the sectored scan with complete consistency, holding each 20-30 degree arc for the full focus time regardless of what the aircraft was doing at the time. The arc sequence was never compressed or abbreviated during high workload phases, and no sector was skipped between sweeps. Every aircraft that entered the searched volume was detected on the first sweep that covered it.
texts.marginal: SP searched the surrounding space arc by arc within the standard, but the arcs widened and the focus time shortened noticeably as task loading increased. Detections were still made, though later in the sweep than a disciplined dwell would have produced. SP is expected to keep the arc width near 20-30 degrees and the focus on a distant point at 3-5 seconds even when the cockpit workload rises.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the sectored visual scan technique, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP searched the surrounding space arc by arc inside the code 1 band, a few sweeps of the canopy compressed into a couple of seconds before the discrete-arc pattern was reestablished. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the arc width near 20-30 degrees and the focus time at 3-5 seconds even when workload rises.
texts_at.2: SP searched the surrounding space arc by arc inside the code 2 band, correcting two or three sectors that had received a passing glance rather than a full search during one maneuver. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice the scan becoming a sweep a little sooner so fewer sectors are affected.
texts_at.3: SP searched the surrounding space one arc at a time, focusing on a distant point within each arc for close to the full 3-5 seconds with only a brief compression during one high-workload maneuver. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold that dwell time steady through that maneuver as well.

texts_above.1: SP searched the surrounding space arc by arc, with a few sweeps of the canopy compressed into a couple of seconds. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the scan had become a sweep during a demanding maneuver and slowed it back to discrete arcs, restoring the dwell without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good sectored scan discipline.
texts_above.3: SP searched the surrounding space one arc of approximately 20-30 degrees at a time, focusing on a distant point within each arc for 3-5 seconds and covering the full field available from the cockpit at a steady rate throughout the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good sectored scan discipline.
texts_above.4: SP applied the sectored scan with complete consistency, holding each arc for the full focus time regardless of workload and detecting every aircraft that entered the searched volume on the first sweep that covered it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent sectored scan discipline.

error_modes.label: REFOCUS ON A DISTANT POINT AFTER THE INSTRUMENT CROSSCHECK

texts.0: SP, due to returning the eyes outside immediately after crosschecking the instruments without refocusing on a distant point, looked out with the eye still focused at the natural resting distance of about 18 inches. The outside checks that followed each crosscheck produced no useful search at all, and converging traffic remained invisible although it was within the sector being looked at. IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft away from an aircraft SP reported as not in sight.
texts.1: SP, due to failing to reestablish distant focus after each instrument crosscheck, cleared the outside sectors with the eye still set for cockpit distance. Almost every outside check that followed a crosscheck was wasted, and traffic was detected only when it was close enough to be picked up by its relative motion, which is at the limit of the standard. SP started deliberately fixing a distant reference before searching only after repeated verbal reminders from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a rapid transition from the instrument crosscheck back outside, did not always refocus on a distant point before beginning the search. Several outside checks were begun with the eye still near the cockpit focus distance, short of the tolerance limit but reducing the value of those checks. SP noticed that distant contacts were not resolving, deliberately picked up a cloud or ground reference first and corrected the habit in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP refocused on a distant point, such as a cloud or a ground reference, after each instrument crosscheck before searching the surrounding space. The eye was reset to distance every time attention returned outside, so each outside check was a genuine search rather than an unfocused look. Contacts at range were resolved on the first sweep after the crosscheck.
texts.4: SP transitioned between the instrument crosscheck and the outside search with the refocus on a distant point built into the transition and never omitted. Distant contacts were resolved immediately on every return outside, with no interval of unfocused looking. The habit held even when the crosscheck was interrupted and resumed under high workload.
texts.marginal: SP refocused on a distant point after the instrument crosscheck within the standard, but the refocus was occasionally rushed when the crosscheck had run long. The first second or two outside was then spent with the eye still set near cockpit distance. SP is expected to fix a distant reference deliberately every time the eyes come out of the cockpit so that no part of the outside check is spent unfocused.

texts_at.0: SP practiced refocusing outside after the instrument crosscheck, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP refocused on a distant point after the instrument crosscheck inside the code 1 band, one outside check beginning with the eye still near the cockpit focus distance before the habit was corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to fix a distant reference deliberately every time the eyes come out of the cockpit.
texts_at.2: SP refocused on a distant point after the instrument crosscheck inside the code 2 band, correcting a check that began without the refocus on one occasion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice unresolved distant contacts a little sooner as the cue to refocus.
texts_at.3: SP refocused on a distant point after each instrument crosscheck before searching the surrounding space, resolving contacts at range on the first sweep with only one transition made a little quickly. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to slow that one transition to match the rest.

texts_above.1: SP refocused on a distant point after the instrument crosscheck, with one outside check beginning while the eye was still near the cockpit focus distance. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP noticed that distant contacts were not resolving after one rushed transition and deliberately picked up a ground reference first, correcting the habit without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound refocus technique after the instrument crosscheck.
texts_above.3: SP refocused on a distant point, such as a cloud or a ground reference, after each instrument crosscheck before searching the surrounding space, resetting the eye to distance every time attention returned outside. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed refocus technique after the instrument crosscheck.
texts_above.4: SP transitioned between the instrument crosscheck and the outside search with the refocus built into the transition and never omitted, resolving distant contacts immediately on every return outside even under high workload. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional refocus technique after the instrument crosscheck.

error_modes.label: DETECTION OF AN AIRCRAFT ON A CONSTANT RELATIVE BEARING

texts.0: SP, due to searching only for movement in the canopy, did not detect an aircraft on a collision course, which by definition appears stationary and is difficult to see. No slight heading change was flown to create the relative movement required for detection although traffic had been called in a known quadrant, and the contact was never acquired. IP took the controls and maneuvered the aircraft off the constant bearing to open separation.
texts.1: SP, due to persisting with a static search of the sector after traffic on a constant relative bearing had been reported, did not use a slight heading change or a wing flash to generate the relative movement needed to acquire it. The aircraft was held on the same heading while the contact grew in the same spot on the canopy, and detection came only at very close range, which is at the limit of the standard. SP flew the heading change only after the IP prompted it verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to searching a reported quadrant without altering the flight path, was slow to acquire an aircraft that remained fixed in the canopy. Several sweeps of the sector produced nothing before the technique was applied, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized the constant bearing, flew a slight heading change to create relative movement and acquired the traffic in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP recognized that an aircraft on a collision course appears stationary in the canopy and used slight heading changes to create the relative movement required for detection. The contact was acquired promptly and its relative motion was then assessed against the canopy reference. Where the traffic was known to be close but not in sight, a wing flash was used to make the aircraft conspicuous to the other pilot.
texts.4: SP treated any reported traffic that could not be seen as a potential constant bearing contact and generated the relative movement needed without prompting. Heading changes were small, flown early and produced acquisition well before separation became a factor. The wing flash was used correctly on the one occasion the traffic was known to be close and still unacquired.
texts.marginal: SP detected traffic on a constant relative bearing within the standard, but the slight heading change was flown only after the static search had already failed for some time. Acquisition was therefore later than the reported position allowed. SP is expected to create the relative movement as soon as a reported contact is not acquired, rather than after several unproductive sweeps of the same sector.

texts_at.0: SP practiced detecting a constant-bearing contact, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP detected an aircraft on a constant relative bearing inside the code 1 band, the contact held on the same heading until the range had closed considerably before the technique was applied. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to create the relative movement as soon as a reported contact is not acquired, rather than after several unproductive sweeps.
texts_at.2: SP detected an aircraft on a constant relative bearing inside the code 2 band, correcting a search of the reported sector that had produced nothing for several sweeps before a heading change was flown. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to fly the heading change a little sooner once the static search has not produced a result.
texts_at.3: SP recognized that an aircraft on a collision course appears stationary in the canopy and used a slight heading change to create the relative movement needed for detection, with acquisition coming promptly on all but one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to apply the technique that promptly on every occasion.

texts_above.1: SP detected an aircraft on a constant relative bearing, with the contact held on the same heading until the range had closed considerably. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a constant bearing contact after a static search had already failed for some sweeps and generated the relative movement needed, acquiring the traffic without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady detection technique for a constant bearing contact.
texts_above.3: SP recognized that an aircraft on a collision course appears stationary in the canopy and used slight heading changes to create the relative movement required for detection, acquiring the contact promptly and assessing its relative motion against the canopy reference. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined detection technique for a constant bearing contact.
texts_above.4: SP treated any reported traffic that could not be seen as a potential constant bearing contact and generated the relative movement needed without prompting, with heading changes flown early enough that acquisition came well before separation became a factor. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate detection technique for a constant bearing contact.

error_modes.label: CLEARING TURNS FOR BLIND SPOTS AND CANOPY BOW RESTRICTIONS

texts.0: SP, due to accepting the field of view available on the established heading and not accounting for the restrictions to visibility created by the canopy bows, did not clear the blind spots beneath the fuselage and the wings. No clearing turn was flown before entering the working area or before commencing maneuvers, so the volume the aircraft was about to occupy was never seen. IP took the controls and cleared the area before the maneuver could be started.
texts.1: SP, due to substituting a head movement for a change of flight path, did not clear the areas masked by the canopy bows and by the fuselage and wings. The clearing turn was reduced to a shallow heading change that exposed almost none of the hidden sectors, which is at the limit of the standard. SP flew a proper clearing turn of approximately 90 degrees off the established heading only after the IP directed it verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to entering the working area with the maneuver sequence already in mind, flew clearing turns that were smaller than needed to expose the blind spots below the aircraft. Part of the area beneath the fuselage and wings remained unseen, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized the omission, flew an additional turn to clear the masked sectors and did so in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP used clearing turns when warranted to clear the blind spots beneath the fuselage and wings, particularly in the training area. The turns were flown with sufficient bank and through approximately 90 degrees off the established heading, and the sectors masked by the canopy bows were checked by moving the head and the flight path together. Each maneuver was commenced only after the volume to be used had been seen.
texts.4: SP cleared the blind areas as a matter of routine, planning the clearing turn as part of the entry to every maneuver rather than as an extra step. Bank angle and heading change were sufficient to expose the sectors beneath the fuselage and wings on both sides, and the canopy bow restrictions were compensated by deliberate head movement. No maneuver was entered into airspace that had not been visually cleared.
texts.marginal: SP flew clearing turns within the standard, but the heading change fell short of what was needed to expose the sectors directly beneath the aircraft. The areas masked by the canopy bows were cleared on one side more thoroughly than the other. SP is expected to size the clearing turn near 90 degrees off heading and to clear both sides equally before commencing the maneuver.

texts_at.0: SP practiced clearing turns for blind spots, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP flew clearing turns for blind spots inside the code 1 band, one turn reduced to a shallow heading change that exposed almost none of the hidden sectors before a full turn was flown. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to size the clearing turn near 90 degrees off heading and to clear both sides equally before commencing the maneuver.
texts_at.2: SP flew clearing turns for blind spots inside the code 2 band, correcting a turn smaller than needed that had left part of the area beneath the aircraft unseen. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to judge the required bank and heading change before entering the working area rather than after.
texts_at.3: SP used clearing turns to clear the blind spots beneath the fuselage and wings, flying them with sufficient bank through approximately 90 degrees off the established heading on all but one entry. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to size that one turn to the same standard as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP flew clearing turns for blind spots, with one turn reduced to a shallow heading change that exposed almost none of the hidden sectors. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a clearing turn that had left part of the area beneath the aircraft unseen and flew an additional turn to clear the masked sectors without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound clearing-turn technique for blind spots.
texts_above.3: SP used clearing turns when warranted to clear the blind spots beneath the fuselage and wings, flying them with sufficient bank through approximately 90 degrees off heading and checking the sectors masked by the canopy bows by moving the head and the flight path together. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise clearing-turn technique for blind spots.
texts_above.4: SP cleared the blind areas as a matter of routine, planning the clearing turn as part of the entry to every maneuver and exposing the sectors beneath the fuselage and wings on both sides without exception. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior clearing-turn technique for blind spots.

error_modes.label: RELIANCE ON ATC AND THE ASSIGNED AREA IN PLACE OF OWN CLEARING

texts.0: SP, due to treating radar monitoring, the assigned flying area and ATC separation as relieving the pilot of the responsibility to clear, did not check the surrounding space to any useful extent. The lookout was effectively delegated to the controlling agency, and an aircraft not known to that agency closed to a hazardous range unseen. IP took the controls and maneuvered the aircraft to reestablish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to the assumption that the assigned area guaranteed deconfliction, cleared only in the direction of flight and only when a call was received. Responsibility for collision avoidance was in practice handed to the controlling agency, and non participating traffic in the same block would not have been detected, which is at the limit of the standard. SP resumed an independent scan only after the IP pointed out verbally that ATC assistance does not relieve the crew of the requirement to clear.
texts.2: SP, due to placing more confidence in radar monitoring than the technique allows, reduced the outside search during the periods when the controlling agency was providing traffic information. Clearing became reactive to calls rather than continuous, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized that each crewmember remains responsible for collision avoidance, resumed the independent scan and did so in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP used radar monitoring, the assigned area and ATC traffic information as aids while retaining full personal responsibility for collision avoidance. The visual search continued at the same rate whether or not traffic information was being provided, and calls were used to narrow the search rather than to replace it. Traffic not known to the controlling agency would have been detected by the scan alone.
texts.4: SP maintained an entirely independent clearing effort throughout, with the services provided by the controlling agency treated purely as additional information. The scan rate showed no change between radar monitored and unmonitored phases of the sortie. Every contact was acquired visually, including those never mentioned on the radio.
texts.marginal: SP retained responsibility for clearing within the standard, but the search visibly relaxed during the phases in which traffic advisories were being provided. Clearing effort rose again as soon as the service ended. SP is expected to hold the scan at the same rate regardless of the assistance available, since radar monitoring and ATC separation do not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to clear.

texts_at.0: SP practiced independent clearing alongside ATC monitoring, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP retained responsibility for clearing inside the code 1 band, the outside search relaxing to a reactive scan while traffic information was being provided before it was resumed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to hold the scan at the same rate regardless of the assistance available, since ATC separation does not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to clear.
texts_at.2: SP retained responsibility for clearing inside the code 2 band, correcting a search that had eased during one period of traffic advisories before the independent scan was resumed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice the reduced search a little sooner so the independent scan is resumed earlier.
texts_at.3: SP used radar monitoring, the assigned area and ATC traffic information as aids while retaining full personal responsibility for collision avoidance, with the visual search continuing at close to the same rate throughout and only a brief easing during one advisory. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold that rate through advisories as well.

texts_above.1: SP retained responsibility for clearing, with the outside search relaxing to a reactive scan while traffic information was being provided. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized that the search had relaxed during a period of traffic advisories and resumed the independent scan without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good independent clearing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP used radar monitoring, the assigned area and ATC traffic information as aids while retaining full personal responsibility for collision avoidance, with the visual search continuing at the same rate whether or not traffic information was being provided. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good independent clearing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an entirely independent clearing effort throughout, with the scan rate showing no change between radar monitored and unmonitored phases and every contact acquired visually including those never mentioned on the radio. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent independent clearing discipline.

error_modes.label: CLEARING ON THE RADIOS AT THE PATTERN CHOKE POINTS

texts.0: SP, due to treating the pattern calls as routine phraseology rather than as position reports essential to deconfliction, did not comply with the mandatory radio transmissions at the choke points. The aircraft passed initial, the downwind and the perch point without any position report, so other traffic in the pattern had no means of predicting the flight path. IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft after a converging aircraft arrived at the same choke point.
texts.1: SP, due to a task sequence in which flying the pattern displaced transmitting, omitted or delayed most of the mandatory calls until the aircraft was already past the choke point concerned. The reports carried no deconfliction value by the time they were made, which is at the limit of the standard. SP made the calls at the correct points only after the IP prompted each one.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the pattern flying task, made some mandatory transmissions late relative to the choke point they refer to. Two calls in the pattern were transmitted after the position had been passed, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized that the calls were slipping, anticipated the remaining choke points and transmitted them correctly in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP complied with the mandatory radio transmissions and made each position report at the choke point it refers to, so that clearing on the radios supported the visual lookout. The known choke points of the pattern were anticipated and the calls were made without prompting. Other pattern traffic had a continuous picture of the aircraft position.
texts.4: SP treated the mandatory transmissions as an integral part of clearing, with every call made at the correct point, in standard phraseology and without displacing the visual scan. The radio picture generated matched the aircraft position exactly at every choke point of the pattern. Adjustments for other traffic were made on the basis of that picture before any conflict developed.
texts.marginal: SP made the mandatory pattern transmissions within the standard, but the calls tended to be triggered by the sight of the reporting point rather than anticipated. Timing slipped slightly at the busiest choke points. SP is expected to anticipate each mandatory call so that the report reaches other pattern traffic before the position is reached rather than as it is passed.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the mandatory pattern position reports, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP made the mandatory pattern transmissions inside the code 1 band, two calls transmitted after the position had already been passed before the timing was corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to anticipate each mandatory call so the report reaches other pattern traffic before the position is reached.
texts_at.2: SP made the mandatory pattern transmissions inside the code 2 band, correcting one call that had been transmitted late relative to its choke point. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to anticipate the busiest choke points a little further ahead so no call slips.
texts_at.3: SP complied with the mandatory radio transmissions and made each position report at the choke point it refers to, anticipating the known choke points of the pattern with only one call trailing by a few seconds. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to anticipate that call as well as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP made the mandatory pattern transmissions, with two calls transmitted after the position had already been passed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized that the calls were slipping relative to the choke points and anticipated the remaining ones, transmitting them correctly without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid radio discipline at pattern choke points.
texts_above.3: SP complied with the mandatory radio transmissions and made each position report at the choke point it refers to, so that clearing on the radios supported the visual lookout and other pattern traffic had a continuous picture of the aircraft position. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed radio discipline at pattern choke points.
texts_above.4: SP treated the mandatory transmissions as an integral part of clearing, with every call made at the correct point in standard phraseology and the radio picture matching the aircraft position exactly at every choke point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional radio discipline at pattern choke points.

error_modes.label: HAZARD CALLOUT AND TAKING CONTROL WHEN COLLISION IS IMMINENT

texts.0: SP, due to hesitation over interrupting the pilot flying, did not point out a hazard immediately after seeing it from the other seat. The traffic was neither called with its clock position and relative motion nor acted upon although time had become critical, and the flight path was not kept well clear of the other aircraft. IP had to take control and avoid the hazard.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting to identify and evaluate the contact before saying anything, called the traffic only when it was already close and gave no clock position or direction of tracking. The information reached the pilot flying too late to be used for anything other than an immediate avoidance, which is at the limit of the standard. SP produced a usable callout only after the IP asked verbally what had been seen.
texts.2: SP, due to a callout delayed while the sighting was confirmed, passed the traffic information later than the situation allowed. The call was made with the correct clock position but after the aircraft had closed appreciably, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized the delay, updated the call with the relative motion and supported the avoidance in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP pointed out the hazard to the pilot flying immediately, using the clock position, the relative height and the direction of tracking. The information was passed as soon as the contact was seen rather than after it was identified, and the resulting flight path was kept well clear of the other aircraft by at least 500 feet. SP was prepared to take control had the collision become imminent.
texts.4: SP called every contact the moment it was acquired, in a form the pilot flying could act on without further questions, and monitored the resulting flight path against the traffic. Separation was preserved throughout with margins well in excess of 500 feet and without any abrupt maneuvering. The readiness to take control if time became critical was evident and correctly restrained.
texts.marginal: SP pointed out hazards to the pilot flying within the standard, but the calls were made after the contact had been identified rather than as soon as it was seen. The resulting separation was adequate although the margin above 500 feet was not large. SP is expected to call the sighting immediately with clock position and tracking, and to refine the description afterwards rather than before speaking.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the hazard callout technique, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP pointed out a hazard to the pilot flying inside the code 1 band, the call following the sighting closely enough that it landed at the limit of the acceptable standard. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to call the sighting immediately with clock position and tracking, refining the description afterward rather than before speaking.
texts_at.2: SP pointed out a hazard to the pilot flying inside the code 2 band, correcting a callout that had been delayed while the sighting was confirmed on one occasion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to pass the clock position the moment the contact is seen rather than after it is confirmed.
texts_at.3: SP pointed out the hazard to the pilot flying immediately on all but one occasion, using the clock position, relative height and direction of tracking, with the flight path kept well clear of the other aircraft throughout. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to call that one contact with the same immediacy.

texts_above.1: SP pointed out a hazard to the pilot flying, the call following the sighting closely enough that it landed at the limit of the acceptable standard. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP updated a delayed call with the relative motion once the sighting was confirmed and supported the avoidance without any intervention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady hazard callout technique.
texts_above.3: SP pointed out the hazard to the pilot flying immediately, using the clock position, the relative height and the direction of tracking, with the information passed as soon as the contact was seen and the resulting flight path kept well clear of the other aircraft. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined hazard callout technique.
texts_above.4: SP called every contact the moment it was acquired in a form the pilot flying could act on without further questions, preserving separation throughout with margins well in excess of the minimum and no abrupt maneuvering. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless hazard callout technique.

error_modes.label: HEAD-DOWN TIME AND THE 80-20 COMPOSITE FLIGHT CROSSCHECK

texts.0: SP, due to over reliance upon instrumentation to maintain aircraft attitude in clear conditions, accumulated head-down time that left almost no capacity to observe other aircraft and hazards. The crosscheck was effectively reversed, with attitude flown from the instruments and the outside world sampled only occasionally, and the aircraft was not trimmed, so control pressures kept attention inside. IP took the controls after traffic converged unseen while SP was head down.
texts.1: SP, due to maintaining attitude from the flight instruments rather than by positioning the nose and wings on the horizon, spent far more than the 20 per cent inside that clear conditions call for. Outside references and clearing received only short interruptions of a continuous head-down crosscheck, which is at the limit of the standard. SP shifted the balance back toward outside references only after repeated verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a failure to trim away the control pressures at the point in the crosscheck where trim is applied, was drawn inside more often than the conditions required. The distribution moved noticeably away from the 80 per cent outside the technique calls for, short of the tolerance limit. SP recognized the drift, trimmed the aircraft and restored the outside weighting of the crosscheck in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained attitude by positioning the nose and wings in relation to the horizon and used the flight instruments to detect the small changes not readily noticed outside. In the clear conditions of the sortie the crosscheck stayed at approximately 80 per cent outside references and clearing and 20 per cent inside, and the aircraft was trimmed so that control pressures did not draw attention into the cockpit. Head-down time never displaced the lookout.
texts.4: SP flew composite throughout, with the horizon as the primary attitude reference and the instruments sampled briefly to confirm it, holding the outside weighting of the crosscheck even during the most demanding parts of the sortie. Trim was applied continuously so that no control pressure competed for attention. Clearing continued without interruption while the flight parameters were held to the accuracy flown.
texts.marginal: SP kept the composite crosscheck within the standard, but the share of time spent on the instruments grew whenever a parameter needed correcting, and the aircraft was left slightly out of trim. Clearing thinned during those periods although it did not stop. SP is expected to trim first and correct from the horizon, so that the outside share of the crosscheck stays near 80 per cent while deviations are being fixed.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the 80/20 composite flight crosscheck, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP flew composite with the crosscheck weighted outside inside the code 1 band, the distribution moving toward the limit of what the standard allows before the balance was restored. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to trim first and correct from the horizon so the outside share of the crosscheck stays near 80 percent while deviations are being fixed.
texts_at.2: SP flew composite with the crosscheck weighted outside inside the code 2 band, correcting a distribution that had drifted noticeably from the 80 percent outside reference during one phase. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to trim away control pressures a little sooner so the drift is smaller.
texts_at.3: SP maintained attitude by positioning the nose and wings in relation to the horizon and used the instruments to detect small changes, keeping the crosscheck close to the 80/20 balance with only a brief drift during one correction.
